newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council ends Jerusalem debate; considers draft.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council ends Jerusalem debate; considers draft.

text.p: The Security Council concluded a two-day debate on Thursday during which virtually all the approximately 50 speakers criticised Israel's decision to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in largely Arab East Jerusalem.
Private consultations were taking place on a resolution proposed by the council's European Union members -- Britain, France, Portugal and Sweden -- but it was uncertain when a vote might take place.

The draft would call on Israel to "refrain from all actions or measures ... which alter the facts on the ground, pre-empt the final status negotiations (between Israel and the Palestinians), and have negative implications for the Middle East peace process."

It would also call on Israel to abide scrupulously by its obligations under the Fourth Geneva Convention, which bars settlements in occupied territories, and would urge all parties to press ahead with the peace process.

The United States, Israel's closest ally and chief sponsor of the Middle East peace process, joined in criticising Israel's decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem that Israel captured during the 1967 Middle East war.
The site is called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians.

But U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson also said the council should take no action that would hamper Middle East peace negotiations, due soon to focus on so-called "final status" issues, including the difficult questions of Jerusalem and Israeli settlements.

Richardson's remarks were widely seen as opposing the adoption of a resolution -- on which Arab delegations and many of their allies have been insisting -- and raised the prospect of either a U.S. abstention or a possible veto. The European Union draft would almost certainly have the support of all 14 other council members.
As an alternative, the United States was believed willing to accept the issuing of an agreed council statement, which carries less weight than a resolution.

A U.S. veto of a resolution could prompt the Arab group, which initiated the council debate, to take the issue to the 185-member General Assembly. There is no veto in the Assembly, whose decisions are not binding.
